design: Randomised clinical trial (3 groups, 3 time points)

items.label: Aim
items.prompt: Find the sentence in the INTRODUCTION stating the objective of the study.
items.model: To assess, through an RCT, the effect of a gratitude intervention on adults' well-being and mental health.
items.why: '…the objective of the present study was…' gives the aim. Notice it is introduced by a justification ('In view of this scarcity…').

items.label: Hypothesis
items.model: Compared with controls, the gratitude group would show greater increases in PA, happiness and life satisfaction and decreases in NA and depression.
items.why: 'The hypothesis was that…'. It continues into the next sentence (change over time).

items.label: Independent variable
items.prompt: What is the independent variable? Name ALL THREE groups.
items.model: Type of daily list: gratitude (intervention) vs hassles vs neutral events (two control groups).
items.why: There is one intervention group and TWO comparison groups.

items.label: Dependent variables
items.prompt: Name at least THREE outcome (dependent) variables.
items.model: Positive affect, negative affect, depression, subjective happiness, life satisfaction.
items.why: The Abstract lists the outcomes analysed.

items.label: Conceptual definition (gratitude)
items.prompt: Find the conceptual definition of GRATITUDE.
items.model: Recognising that something good happened, plus an appraisal that someone or something (a person, nature, a divine entity) was responsible.
items.why: 'In general terms, gratitude stems from…' defines the concept.

items.label: Conceptual definition (well-being)
items.prompt: Find the sentences that define the TWO dimensions of subjective well-being. Select the one that explains what each dimension is.
items.model: Cognitive = life satisfaction; emotional = prevalence of positive over negative affect.
items.why: Sentence 1 names the two dimensions; sentence 2 explains them.

items.label: Operational definition (life satisfaction)
items.model: The 5-item Satisfaction With Life Scale (7-point Likert).
items.why: Each instrument has its own small subsection; find the SWLS.

items.label: Research gap
items.prompt: Find a sentence that shows what is missing or weak in previous gratitude research.
items.model: Most studies were done in North America and Europe (and many had weak comparison groups).
items.why: Two problems are raised: methodological issues with comparison groups, and a lack of non-Western samples.

items.label: General method
options: Randomised clinical trial with repeated measures
items.ans: Randomised clinical trial with repeated measures
items.model: RCT: random assignment to 3 groups, measured at 3 times.
items.why: Random allocation (Research Randomizer) plus measures before, after and at follow-up.

items.label: Sampling method
items.prompt: Find the sentence stating the SAMPLING method used to recruit participants.
items.model: Non-probabilistic convenience sampling, until at least 315 participants were reached.
items.why: Random ASSIGNMENT (to groups) is not the same as random SAMPLING (choosing who takes part). This study used convenience sampling.

items.label: Blinding
items.prompt: Find the sentence explaining what participants did NOT know (single-blind).
items.model: Participants didn't know there were three groups or which group they were in.

items.label: Attrition
items.prompt: How many participants were randomised, and how many were finally analysed?
items.model: 1,337 randomised; only 410 analysed (927 stopped sending lists, 10 withdrew).
items.why: Very high attrition (dropout) is common in online interventions and is a key limitation.

items.label: Who dropped out?
items.prompt: Find the sentence showing that dropouts differed from completers in well-being scores.
items.model: Dropouts had higher NA and depression and lower PA, happiness and life satisfaction.
items.why: If dropouts differ from completers, the final sample may not represent everyone who started. This is a threat to generalisability.

items.label: Was the hypothesis supported?
items.prompt: The hypothesis predicted the gratitude group would improve MORE than the control groups on all outcomes. Was it supported?
items.model: Partly: gratitude beat BOTH controls only for positive affect; on the other outcomes it was similar to the neutral-events group.
items.why: Improving over time isn't enough; the hypothesis required a bigger change than the control groups.

items.label: Explaining an unexpected result
items.prompt: Find the sentence explaining WHY the neutral-events group improved almost as much as the gratitude group.
items.model: Neutral-events participants tended to list positive events, making their task similar to the gratitude task.
items.why: Authors often use qualitative observations to explain unexpected quantitative findings.

items.label: Comparison group issue
items.prompt: Find the sentence explaining why comparing gratitude with a HASSLES group can be misleading.
items.model: We can't tell whether gratitude helped or the negative hassles task made people feel worse.
items.why: This is about choosing a fair control group: a negative control can exaggerate an intervention's effect.

items.label: Limitation (dropout)
items.prompt: Find the limitation about LOSS TO FOLLOW-UP.
items.model: Loss to follow-up; high dropout is expected in self-performed online interventions.
items.why: 'Another limitation…' introduces it, and the next sentence explains why.

items.label: Future research
items.prompt: Find a suggestion for future research about intervention FORMAT.
items.model: Investigate which characteristics make online interventions work better (intensity, duration, format).
items.why: Future research directions are in the 'Future Outlooks' subsection, not labelled 'future research'.

items.label: Practical implication
items.prompt: Find a sentence describing the practical value of a gratitude list.
items.model: It's a simple, cheap, easy and pleasant intervention that could be used with many audiences.
items.why: Practical value is described in terms of cost and ease of use.
